note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

msa.note: Maged (ar_SA) reading each letter's own Arabic name. For letter names the modern standard and the classical values coincide, so this is both the living pronunciation and the historical one — there is no second system to offer.

0.why: The Arabic name read by an Arabic voice: initial hamzat qaṭʿ gives a true glottal stop, then a short [a], then [lif]. The vowels are written in because the bare spelling ألف is ambiguous with أَلْف, 'a thousand' — and the voice was in fact taking it that way: the undiacritised string rendered 3300 bytes shorter, one syllable's worth.
0.compromise: None in the name. But note that the name is not the sound: alif itself has no consonantal value — it is either the seat of a hamza or the carrier of a long ā — so this clip demonstrates the letter's title, not its function.

1.why: A plain voiced bilabial stop, a long [aː], and a final glottal stop. Arabic b is unaspirated, which an English voice saying 'ba' would not give.

2.why: Maged is ar_SA, and the Saudi/standard value of ج is the affricate [dʒ] — 'j as in judge', exactly as this hall states. The kasra is written in because the bare spelling جيم came back 4180 bytes short, the voice reading a short vowel where the name has a long [iː].
2.compromise: This letter is the one real regional fork in the alphabet: [dʒ] in the standard and the Gulf, a hard [ɡ] in Egypt and much of Sudan and Yemen, [ʒ] in the Levant and the Maghreb. Only the standard [dʒ] is offered here, because no Egyptian or Levantine voice is installed and faking [ɡ] with an Italian voice would break the hall's single-voice integrity for one letter.

3.why: Voiced stop, long [aː], plain [l]. No final hamza on this name, and none is rendered.
3.compromise: The hall calls Arabic d dental, the tongue against the teeth. Whether the synthesiser's [d] is truly dental rather than alveolar is not something the model exposes; the contrast is subtle and no listener will be misled.

4.why: A genuine [h] onset — Arabic sounds h in every position, and an Arabic voice will not swallow it. The final hamza was verified present: هاء renders 9020 bytes longer than ها.
4.compromise: None of consequence. The clip cannot demonstrate the hall's point that hāʾ is sounded word-finally too, since the name puts it initially.

5.why: Glide, long [aː], glide again — the letter's own sound bracketing its name. The fatḥa is written in as insurance against the voice reading the initial و as the conjunction wa- plus a stray 'āw'; testing showed vocalised and bare spellings render byte-identical here, so the insurance costs nothing.

6.why: Voiced [z] and a final [j] glide, closing the syllable rather than becoming a vowel — an Arabic voice takes final yāʾ after fatḥa as a diphthong offglide, which is correct.

7.why: The whole reason this hall uses a native voice. [ħ], the voiceless pharyngeal fricative, exists in no other installed language; every European voice would substitute a plain [h] and destroy the contrast with hāʾ at index 4. Slowed to 150 wpm so the constriction is audible as a sustained rasp and not a flick.
7.compromise: Concatenative synthesis reproduces a pharyngeal well when the unit inventory contains it, and Maged's does. The one honest caveat is that the degree of constriction in a synthesised [ħ] tends to be shallower than a careful reciter's.

8.why: The emphatic t, with the pharyngealisation and — the part that actually carries the contrast for a listener — the backed, darkened [ɑː] that follows it. Compare tāʾ at index 21 to hear what emphasis does to a vowel. Slowed so the vowel colour is audible.
8.compromise: IPA is given as [tˤaːʔ] for consistency with the transliteration, but what you will hear is nearer [tˤɑːʔ]: the emphatic backs the vowel, and that backing is the perceptual cue, not the consonant itself.

9.why: Palatal glide onset, long [aː], final hamza. Verified against يا: the hamza adds 9020 bytes.

10.why: A plain velar [k], deliberately NOT the uvular of qāf. Heard against index 18 this is the clearest available demonstration of the kāf/qāf contrast, which is the single distinction European learners most often collapse.
10.compromise: Arabic k is unaspirated in careful speech; a synthesised initial stop may carry a little more release noise than a native speaker's.

11.why: Clear (non-velarised) [l] in an Arabic voice's own phonology, which is the right value for lām in isolation.
11.compromise: The hall notes that lām darkens to a velarised [ɫ] in the name Allāh. That allophone is not audible here, and this clip should not be taken as evidence about it.

12.why: Bilabial nasal either side of a long [iː]. The kasra is written in for parity with jīm; here it made no measurable difference to the rendering, the vocalised and bare forms being byte-identical.

13.why: Alveolar nasal either side of a long [uː]. Vocalised and bare spellings render identically; the ḍamma is kept for legibility to a reader looking at the string.

14.why: A plain voiceless [s] with no emphasis and, as the hall insists, no voicing to [z] — an Arabic voice will not intervocalically voice it the way a German or Spanish reading might.

15.why: The voiced pharyngeal, the sound the hall calls the hardest in Arabic for European speakers, and one that literally cannot be approximated by any other installed voice — Italian, German, English and Russian would all simply delete it and leave the word beginning with a vowel. The sukūn is written on the yāʾ to hold the [aj] as a diphthong rather than letting it break into two syllables. Slowed to 150 so the constriction and its creaky voicing can be heard.
15.compromise: A synthesised [ʕ] is the least reliable segment in this hall. Concatenative units for it exist in Maged's inventory, but the pharyngeal is heavily coarticulated in real speech and a spliced rendering tends to sound like a strongly creaky vowel onset rather than a fully constricted pharyngeal. Expect something recognisably right, not something a reciter would accept.

17.why: Emphatic s. Play it directly against sīn at index 14: same consonant, different tongue posture, and a completely different vowel colour after it. Slowed so that colour is audible.
17.compromise: As with ṭāʾ, the transcription [sˤaːd] understates what you hear; the vowel is backed toward [ɑː], and it is the vowel, not the sibilant, that a non-Arabic ear will actually register. Note too that the d following an emphatic is itself somewhat darkened.

18.why: The uvular stop, made far back against the uvula and quite distinct from kāf. Maged has it as a genuine phoneme; no European voice does, and substituting an English or Italian [k] would erase the distinction the hall is at pains to draw.
18.compromise: Regionally qāf is [ɡ] across the Gulf and Bedouin dialects, [ʔ] in Cairo, Beirut and Damascus, and [k] in parts of Palestine. This clip gives the standard uvular value only, which is the value used in reciting the alphabet everywhere.

19.why: An alveolar tap or trill — the hall says 'as in Italian', and Arabic r is the same articulation. No English voice could give it; an Arabic voice gives it natively.
19.compromise: Whether the synthesised r comes out as a single tap or a full trill is not controllable from the text, and initial rāʾ in Arabic is usually a tap rather than the multi-contact trill.

20.why: Postalveolar fricative and long [iː]. Straightforward, and identical in the standard and every dialect.

21.why: The point of this clip is what it does NOT have: the English puff of breath. Arabic initial t is unaspirated and dental, and only a native voice will deliver it that way — an English 'tah' would give [tʰ], which is a different sound in this system.
21.compromise: Dental versus alveolar place is not verifiable from the synthesiser's output, and a concatenative initial stop can carry slightly more aspiration noise than a careful native speaker.

22.why: The voiceless interdental of English 'think', which Maged has natively — this is one of the few letters an English voice could also have managed, but consistency of voice across the hall is worth more than the alternative.
22.compromise: In much of the Levantine and Egyptian colloquial ث merges with [t] or [s]. The standard interdental given here is the value used in reciting the alphabet and in reading the Qurʾān.

23.why: The voiceless velar/uvular fricative of Scots 'loch'. Spanish j or Russian х could have produced something close, but they would also have brought the wrong vowel and no final hamza; the Arabic voice gives the sound and the name together. Slowed so the friction is sustained.
23.compromise: Arabic خ is usually described as post-velar or uvular [χ] rather than plain velar [x]; the transcription follows the hall's own convention. The audible difference is small.

24.why: The voiced interdental of English 'this' — the pair to thāʾ at index 22, and best heard immediately after it.
24.compromise: As with thāʾ, colloquial registers frequently merge ذ with [d] or [z]; the standard interdental is given.

25.why: The emphatic d, and the letter Arabic names itself after — lughat al-ḍād, 'the language of the ḍād'. The name puts the sound at both ends of the word, so the clip demonstrates it twice. Slowed so the backed vowel between them is clear.
25.compromise: This clip gives the MODERN value, an emphatic alveolar stop. The sound Sībawayhi describes — made along the side of the tongue against the molars, a pharyngealised lateral — is not what you will hear, and cannot be synthesised by any installed voice. The hall's own entry makes that distinction; this recipe can only honour half of it.

26.why: The emphatic interdental — dhāl with the tongue drawn back and the vowel darkened. An ar_SA voice is essential here: the Saudi standard keeps the interdental articulation that the hall states.
26.compromise: The weakest guarantee in the hall, and marked accordingly. ظ is realised as an emphatic [zˤ] rather than [ðˤ] across Egypt and much of the Levant, and it is not possible to verify by inspection which of the two Maged's unit inventory actually contains. If the clip sounds like a darkened z rather than a darkened th, that is the merger, not an error in the name — but it would not be the value this hall states.

27.why: The voiced counterpart of khāʾ, which the hall compares to the guttural r of Parisian French. French Thomas could have produced something in the neighbourhood, but the French sound is uvular and often devoiced, and it would have brought French vowels with it; the Arabic voice gives the true voiced velar/uvular fricative and the correct [aj] diphthong. Slowed so the voicing is audible against khāʾ.
27.compromise: Like khāʾ, غ is usually nearer uvular [ʁ] than velar [ɣ]; the transcription follows the hall's convention, and the audible difference is small.
